title: Know Your Customer Technical Reference
readerIntent: Understand the KYC capability, its Axis management surface, extension model, current maturity, and high-sensitivity governance requirements.
priorKnowledge: Understand customer identity, workflows, providers, security, audit, and retention.
owner: gCompliance/kyc; complianceCore owns shared governance and Profile retains customer identity ownership
summary: KYC coordinates verification cases, evidence references, checks, decisions, provider interactions, and audit without duplicating customer identity or exposing sensitive evidence broadly.

sections.heading: Start here for business users
items: Authorized employees use the single Axis Compliance Management section for KYC cases, review queues, subject status, masked document metadata, policies and requirements, providers, and audit evidence.
Axis displays backend-published pages and actions only. It does not decide eligibility, approve a case, store identity evidence, choose a provider, or bypass maker-checker rules.

A missing page or action normally means the capability, feature state, tenant context, or employee permission is not effective; administrators should inspect backend configuration and authorization rather than adding a frontend shortcut.

For decision makers, the value is one reusable identity-verification authority across onboarding, checkout, payment, refund, and order lifecycle. The trade-off is that jurisdiction, provider, privacy, legal, infrastructure, and operational qualification remain customer responsibilities.

sections.heading: Authority and case model
items: The KYC capability owns cases, requirements, checks, evidence metadata, consent references, decisions, expiry, review, and audit; Profile owns customer identity.
A case binds tenant, customer, purpose, jurisdiction, policy/version, required checks, status, owner, dates, and safe provider references.
Raw documents and biometrics use approved secure storage and access policy; ordinary models, logs, search, events, and frontend state contain only necessary metadata.

sections.heading: Verification lifecycle
items: Submission resolves authenticated tenant, enterprise, subject, entry point, consent, dynamic policy, required documents, private nMedia references, and idempotency before atomically creating or reconciling profile, case, consent, document, and audit evidence.

Automatic provider checks and manual reviewer actions coexist through Pipeline and Workflow. Normalized checks and append-only decisions project case/profile state; KYC owns final state and target authorization.

Manual review supports assignment, claim, takeover, information request, escalation, SLA, maker submission, independent checker approval or rejection, override, reversal, high-risk approval, policy exception, close, and expiry.

A scheduled CronJob-owned lifecycle marks expiry and re-verification, notifies the subject, continues Workflow, audits outcomes, coordinates legal hold, and asks nMedia to delete elapsed document content.

sections.heading: Provider boundary
items: Adapters receive minimum required data through configured endpoints and secret references, normalize provider status and errors, and never expose vendor SDKs to Profile or clients.

Timeout after submission creates an uncertain check reconciled by provider reference before retry; completed execution evidence makes repeated calls idempotent. Retry classification, exponential bounded backoff, readiness, sandbox/live guard, circuit opening, and failover are persisted and observable.

Webhooks require raw-body cryptographic verification, provider/account/tenant mapping, current or rotated secret reference, timestamp tolerance, unique provider event identity, and replay rejection before normalization.

The included mock provider is deterministic test evidence, not a production provider. A real provider remains project-selected and requires credentials, licensing, jurisdiction, residency, live guards, security review, load, outage, callback, reconciliation, and deletion evidence.

sections.heading: Privacy and security
items: Enforce purpose limitation, consent, encryption, field masking, least privilege, separation of duties, residency, retention, deletion, legal hold, access review, and incident response.
Public responses do not reveal detailed fraud signals, document data, provider payloads, credentials, reviewer notes, or whether another customer's case exists.
Service callbacks authenticate source, bind tenant and case, validate replay and signature, and cannot directly update Profile credentials.

sections.heading: Verification and operations
items: Test valid and invalid identity, wrong tenant, missing consent, duplicate case, document boundaries, provider timeout, webhook replay, manual override, appeal, expiry, and revocation.
Test cross-role access, masking, retention/deletion, provider outage, uncertain reconciliation, workflow recovery, audit integrity, migration, load, and regression.
Monitor case age, check latency, provider error, manual backlog, expiry, unresolved uncertainty, access, deletion, and incidents with legal and operational ownership.

sections.heading: Contract
items: Tenant/customer reference, case, requirement, check, provider reference, evidence metadata, consent, decision, expiry, reviewer, status, reason, and audit.
Provider adapters receive minimum required data through governed secrets and endpoints; raw evidence storage and access follow project legal/security policy.
Manual and automatic actions use Workflow where configured; target KYC services own decisions.
Profile remains identity authority and references KYC status through governed contracts rather than copied credentials/evidence.

sections.heading: Configuration and customer customization
items: Framework defaults resolve through Nodics project, environment, server, node, tenant, and customer layers. Customer modules override only owned differences such as verification levels, exact minor-unit thresholds, jurisdiction and risk rules, document requirements, consent, expiry, retention, masking, permissions, rate windows, providers, workflows, and Axis presentation metadata.

Add provider integrations beneath the provider-neutral KYC adapter contract. Keep credentials in governed secret references and keep vendor payloads out of KYC records, logs, events, search, Axis, and generated documentation.

Add new compliance domains as siblings under gCompliance and attach their authorized Axis pages to compliance-management. Do not copy KYC into a customer module, add a second compliance console, or move lifecycle authority into Axis.

Meaningful services, provider adapters, policy resolution, Pipeline nodes, Workflow definitions, rate limits, schedules, and metadata are replaceable from later customer modules. Preserve service names/contracts or contribute a later configured selector; never edit framework defaults for one customer.

Rollback removes the later customer contribution or provider activation and restores inherited defaults; it must not delete or rewrite regulated evidence. Re-run structure, generated context, focused contracts, cross-capability tests, Axis tests, and environment journeys after every override.

sections.heading: Beginner tutorial: verify one customer
items: 1. Upload each required document through a private nMedia folder bound to the kycDocuments purpose, enterprise, subject owner, MIME/size policy, retention boundary, and no reuse.

2. Submit the case with tenant, enterprise, CUSTOMER subject, entry point, idempotency key, correlation ID, accepted consent version, and nMedia codes. A repeat with the same scoped idempotency key returns the same case.

3. In Axis Compliance Management, open KYC Cases. Use detail panels for normalized checks, masked documents, review tasks, decisions, provider attempts, and redacted audit. Never request raw provider or file paths.
4. If review is required, claim or assign the task, record only bounded safe notes, request an independent checker where policy requires it, and complete an authorized explicit action.
5. The consuming capability requests an expiring eligibility decision. It stores only the decision reference and honors invalidation; it never accepts a caller-supplied KYC profile.

sections.heading: Operations, security, recovery, and release evidence
items: Monitor case and review age, SLA breach, provider readiness/error/latency/circuit, callback rejection/replay, retry and recovery, eligibility denial, rate rejection, sensitive access, lifecycle deletion/hold, notification failure, Workflow stall, and audit persistence.

Backup KYC database and nMedia metadata/content consistently, protect keys and secret references separately, test point-in-time restore in isolation, reconcile restored cases/provider events/media before reopening traffic, and never restore deleted content across a legal deletion boundary without approved legal authority.

Incident response must preserve immutable evidence, revoke or rotate affected service/provider credentials, pause live calls or schedules through configuration, bound customer communication, reconcile uncertain provider outcomes, and record approval before recovery.

Production evidence includes data minimization, encryption, masking, purpose and consent, residency, retention/deletion/legal hold, role and tenant isolation, provider qualification, duplicate/replay/concurrency, maker-checker, outage/reconciliation, backup/restore, load, accessibility, audit integrity, incident response, legal review, and full regression.

Implementation evidence is not certification. Do not describe the customer solution or a real provider as production-ready until its jurisdiction-specific legal, privacy, security, infrastructure, provider, performance, recovery, and independent assurance gates pass.

sections.heading: Technical reference
items: Primary intent routes: submit case, case action, review-task action, document delivery, eligibility evaluation, signed provider webhook, provider configuration action, provider-policy action, and operations dashboard. All are secured and permissioned; generated KYC schema CRUD is private.

Primary configuration families: kyc.policy, kyc.documents, kyc.persistence, kyc.eligibility, kyc.providerExecution, kyc.providerWebhook, kyc.workflows, kyc.lifecycle, kyc.rateLimit, kyc.operations, and compliance.kycEnforcement.

Stable ownership: gCompliance/complianceCore composes shared governance and Axis root; gCompliance/kyc owns KYC; Profile owns identities; nMedia owns binary lifecycle; Workflow owns long-running execution; CronJob owns scheduling; Notification owns delivery; consumer modules own their business lifecycle.

Verification commands: run focused Compliance/KYC/nMedia/Notification/Order contracts, npm run llm:generate then npm run llm:validate, npm run structure:audit, backend basic tests, nodicsaxis verify, nodicsdocs generate/verify, and explicitly enabled environment E2E suites.
